The single large positive eigenvalue, in the accent color, signals a two-way community split." width="100%"} The eigenvalues of `modularity_matrix()`, in increasing order. Large positive eigenvalues signal community structure: `k` clearly positive eigenvalues suggest about `k + 1` communities (one positive eigenvalue already means a good two-way split), and the leading eigenvector gives the best two-way split by modularity. On a directed graph the modularity matrix is not symmetric and its eigenvalues can be complex. Matches NetworkX's `modularity_spectrum()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The eigenvalues in increasing order (by real part, then imaginary part, if complex): `float` values on undirected graphs, `complex` on directed ones. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two dense groups give one large positive eigenvalue, the signal of a two-way split (two communities): ::: {#bf6ece99 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list("ABCDEF")) graph.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D")]) [round(v, 3) for v in graph.modularity_spectrum()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [-1.732, -1.0, -1.0, -0.429, -0.0, 1.732] ``` ::: :::
